# MOVEit Transfer / CL0P Mass Exploitation Investigation Report

**Assessment date:** October 1, 2026  
**Scope:** Trace exploitation of CVE-2023-34362 from disclosure through LEMURLOOT deployment, attribution to FIN11, and linkage to CL0P-related extortion infrastructure.  
**Sources used:**  
- **S1:** Mandiant/Google Cloud report, “Zero-Day Vulnerability in MOVEit Transfer Exploited for Data Theft,” supplied through the CISA URL.  
- **S2:** NIST National Vulnerability Database entry for CVE-2023-34362.

## Executive assessment

The available evidence supports the conclusion that CVE-2023-34362 was a critical, unauthenticated SQL-injection vulnerability in Progress MOVEit Transfer that was exploited in the wild beginning no later than May 27, 2023. The exploitation chain described by Mandiant involved SQL-injection activity against the MOVEit `guestaccess.aspx` endpoint, deployment of the LEMURLOOT web shell under filenames designed to resemble legitimate MOVEit components, enumeration of files and folders, retrieval of configuration and Azure Blob Storage information, and theft of large volumes of files. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a); [S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

Mandiant initially tracked the activity as UNC4857 but reported on June 9, 2023 that it had merged UNC4857 into FIN11. The stated basis was overlap in targeting, infrastructure, certificates, and the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site. The evidence therefore supports **Mandiant’s assessment of FIN11 attribution**, but attribution should remain qualified as an analytic judgment rather than an independently proven identity. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

The extortion connection is also supported, but in stages. Mandiant reported that victims did not initially receive ransom demands. On June 6, 2023, however, the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site claimed responsibility and threatened publication of stolen data unless victims paid an extortion fee. Historical overlap with FIN11 activity involving Accellion FTA and GoAnywhere MFT further supported the FIN11/CL0P assessment. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## Source reliability and evidentiary limits

### Source hierarchy

S1 is a detailed threat-intelligence and incident-response report authored by Mandiant analysts and hosted in the supplied material through a CISA advisory URL. It provides technical observations, malware analysis, attribution reasoning, infrastructure observations, and an account of the public CL0P^_-LEAKS claim. Its strongest evidentiary value concerns observed intrusion behavior and malware functionality. Attribution statements are explicitly presented as Mandiant’s analysis and should therefore be described as an assessment.

S2 is the NVD record for CVE-2023-34362. It provides the vulnerability description, severity, affected-product information, weakness classification, exploitation status, vendor reference, and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities information. S2 is strongest for vulnerability metadata and affected-version records. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

### Limitations

The supplied material does not provide a complete victim list, a definitive count of affected organizations, complete network telemetry, or direct forensic evidence from every alleged victim. Mandiant expressly stated that the campaign’s impact was probably broader than the incidents it had directly observed. The supplied evidence also does not independently establish that every incident involving CVE-2023-34362 was conducted by FIN11 or that every CL0P-branded claim was authored by the same operational group. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## Chronology of the exploitation campaign

| Date or period | Event | Evidentiary status |
|---|---|---|
| May 19–22, 2023 | Certificates on several operational hosts were generated; Mandiant assessed this as suggestive of infrastructure staging. | Mandiant observation and assessment ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)) |
| May 27, 2023 | Earliest evidence of exploitation identified in Mandiant incident-response engagements; web shells and data theft followed. | Mandiant observation ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)) |
| May 28, 2023 | Multiple `human2.aspx` LEMURLOOT samples appeared in VirusTotal. | Mandiant observation ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)) |
| May 31, 2023 | Progress Software publicly announced the critical MOVEit vulnerability. | Reported in S1 and reflected in S2’s vendor reference ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a); [S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362)) |
| June 2, 2023 | CVE-2023-34362 was published in the NVD; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog with a June 23 remediation deadline. | NVD record ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362)) |
| June 5, 2023 | Bleeping Computer reported that an individual affiliated with CLOP claimed responsibility for incidents involving exploitation of MOVEit. | Secondary report summarized by Mandiant; not independently supplied as a separate source ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)) |
| June 6, 2023 | CL0P^_-LEAKS claimed responsibility and threatened publication of stolen data unless victims paid. | Mandiant observation ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)) |
| June 9, 2023 | Mandiant reported merging UNC4857 into FIN11. | Mandiant attribution update ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)) |

The chronology indicates that exploitation preceded public disclosure. The earliest exploitation identified by Mandiant occurred on May 27, four days before Progress’s May 31 announcement and six days before NVD publication on June 2. This temporal sequence is consistent with a genuine zero-day exploitation period, although the supplied evidence does not establish when the vulnerability was first discovered by the operators. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a); [S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

## Vulnerability and initial access

CVE-2023-34362 was classified as CWE-89, improper neutralization of special elements used in an SQL command. NVD assigned a CVSS 3.1 score of **9.8 Critical**, with the vector `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`. This describes a remotely exploitable vulnerability requiring no privileges or user interaction and having potentially high confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

The NVD description states that an unauthenticated attacker could gain access to the MOVEit Transfer database and, depending on the database engine, infer database structure and contents or execute SQL statements that alter or delete database elements. Exploitation could occur over HTTP or HTTPS. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

Mandiant observed POST requests to the legitimate `guestaccess.aspx` file before interaction with LEMURLOOT. Mandiant interpreted this sequence as evidence that the SQL-injection attacks were directed at that endpoint. The supplied material does not include the exact injection strings or a complete request-by-request forensic transcript, so the endpoint and sequence should be treated as reported observations rather than independently reconstructed facts. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## LEMURLOOT deployment and functionality

Following exploitation, the operators deployed a C# web shell called **LEMURLOOT**. The web shell was given filenames such as `human2.aspx` and `_human2.aspx`, which masqueraded as `human.aspx`, a legitimate MOVEit Transfer component. This naming choice could make malicious files less conspicuous during routine inspection. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

Mandiant described the operational sequence as rapid. In some cases, data theft occurred within minutes of web-shell deployment. This supports an assessment that the campaign was optimized for automated or semi-automated exploitation and collection rather than prolonged interactive intrusion in every observed case. However, the report does not establish that all victims experienced the same timing. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

LEMURLOOT authenticated incoming requests through a hard-coded password represented by a 36-character GUID-formatted value. It checked for the `X-siLock-Comment` header and returned HTTP 404 to clients that failed authentication. A successful connection received an `X-siLock-Comment` response with the value `comment`. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

The web shell parsed tasking from the HTTP headers `X-siLock-Step1`, `X-siLock-Step2`, and `X-siLock-Step3`. Its documented capabilities included:

- Retrieving MOVEit Azure configuration information, including the Azure Blob Storage account, key, and container.
- Querying file, file-size, folder, owner, and institution information.
- Downloading files from the local MOVEit system.
- Creating a MOVEit user with the login and real name `Health Check Service`.
- Deleting the same user.
- Compressing returned data with gzip.
- Connecting to the MOVEit SQL database using settings obtained from the application. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

The `X-siLock-Step1` value `-1` caused LEMURLOOT to retrieve Azure settings and file-related metadata. The value `-2` caused deletion of users whose real name was `Health Check Service`. Other values were used with `X-siLock-Step2` and `X-siLock-Step3` to identify file and folder data for retrieval or to create an account and insert it into an active MOVEit session. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

This capability set demonstrates that the web shell was not merely a generic command shell. It was tailored to MOVEit’s application structure and database schema, enabling collection of stored files and information needed to locate them. Mandiant reported multiple cases involving theft of large volumes of files. It also noted that Azure Blob credentials and storage details could be extracted, creating a potential pathway to data stored outside the local appliance. The supplied report does not prove that all Azure credentials were subsequently used or that all cloud-hosted data was exfiltrated. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## Infrastructure and operational pattern

Mandiant identified repeated scanning and exploitation from addresses in the `5.252.188.0/22` range. It emphasized that web-shell interaction and data theft originated from different systems, indicating separation between initial exploitation infrastructure and later collection infrastructure. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

Several systems used for second-stage operations hosted RDP on TCP port 3389. Their certificates had been generated between May 19 and May 22, which Mandiant considered suggestive of infrastructure staging. This is an infrastructure correlation, not proof that the certificate creators, RDP operators, web-shell operators, and extortion actors were personally identical. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

Mandiant also reported that an IP address attempting exploitation had previously been used by FIN11 as early as mid-January 2023. The system had hosted RDP and continued presenting the same X.509 certificate when later used in the MOVEit activity. Mandiant treated these overlaps, together with shared ISPs, netblocks, and IP addresses, as attribution evidence. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## Attribution to FIN11 and linkage to CL0P

Mandiant initially attributed the activity to UNC4857. On June 6, 2023, it merged UNC4857 into FIN11 based on four stated categories of overlap:

1. Targeting.
2. Infrastructure.
3. Certificates.
4. The CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

The attribution is strengthened by Mandiant’s comparison with previous FIN11-attributed campaigns. The report identifies exploitation of Accellion’s legacy File Transfer Appliance from late 2020 through early 2021, where actors deployed the DEWMODE web shell, and exploitation of GoAnywhere MFT vulnerability CVE-2023-0669 in early 2023. In both comparisons, the common operational theme was exploitation of file-transfer technology followed by data theft and extortion activity. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

The CL0P connection is supported by the June 6 post on the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site claiming responsibility and threatening publication of stolen data. Mandiant stated that this was consistent with prior FIN11-attributed data-theft extortion. Nevertheless, the supplied evidence establishes a public claim and correlation, not cryptographic proof of site control or a complete organizational identity between FIN11 and every actor using the CLOP/CL0P name. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## Contradictions and version considerations

There is a material version-description discrepancy within the supplied evidence. The early NVD description lists fixed versions as 2021.0.6, 2021.1.4, 2022.0.4, 2022.1.5, and 2023.0.1, while the later affected-configuration data lists affected ranges ending before 2021.0.7, 2021.1.5, 2022.0.5, 2022.1.6, and 2023.0.2. The later records also identify additional MOVEit Transfer and MOVEit Cloud ranges. This may reflect revised vendor version mapping or correction of the initial record, but the supplied evidence does not explain the discrepancy. For remediation decisions, the later affected-configuration records and current vendor guidance should be preferred, while historical reporting should preserve the discrepancy. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

The NVD page also shows a future-dated modification record of June 17, 2026 in the supplied capture. Because the requested assessment date is October 1, 2026, that record is temporally possible, but the supplied material provides no additional context about the change. It should not be interpreted beyond the metadata displayed in S2. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

## Final judgment

The most defensible judgment is that the MOVEit campaign was a large-scale exploitation and data-theft operation conducted through a purpose-built intrusion chain: unauthenticated SQL injection, deployment of the MOVEit-specific LEMURLOOT web shell, discovery and extraction of stored files and cloud-storage configuration, and subsequent extortion activity. The activity began before public disclosure, was technically tailored to MOVEit, and used infrastructure with reported overlaps to prior FIN11 operations. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a); [S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

Mandiant’s attribution of UNC4857 to FIN11 is supported by multiple independent correlation categories reported in S1, and the CL0P^_-LEAKS claim provides a public extortion linkage. The appropriate confidence level is **high for the vulnerability and malware sequence, moderate-to-high for the FIN11 assessment, and moderate for the direct identity relationship between FIN11 and the CL0P branding**, because the supplied evidence does not independently verify the operators behind the leak site. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## References

Mandiant. (2023, June 2). *Zero-day vulnerability in MOVEit Transfer exploited for data theft*. Google Cloud Blog. [CISA-hosted source URL](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)

National Institute of Standards and Technology. (2023, June 2). *CVE-2023-34362 detail*. National Vulnerability Database. [NVD source URL](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362)
